summary: Parents of young people who died after buying counterfeit, fentanyl-laced pills on Snapchat are suing Snap, arguing the app's design facilitates drug sales to minors. Snap has moved to dismiss under Section 230, while some bereaved parents, such as Ed Ternan, choose collaboration with Snap and education over litigation. The article follows several families' experiences and their advocacy work.
one_line: Over 65 families sue Snap over fentanyl-laced counterfeit pills bought on Snapchat, while some parents instead pursue education and partnership with the company.
key_facts: Brooke Badger, 17, was found dead on 17 June 2021 at her California home after taking a counterfeit pill she believed was Roxicet; it contained a lethal dose of fentanyl.
Nationally, opioid overdose deaths among people 24 and under nearly doubled from 2019-2021.
In California, fentanyl-related overdose deaths among 15- to 19-year-olds rose nearly 800% between 2018 and 2021, per the California Overdose Surveillance Dashboard.
In April, relatives of more than 65 victims, represented by the Social Media Victims Law Center, filed lawsuits against Snap, Snapchat's parent company.
Lead attorney Matthew Bergman says Snapchat's messages disappear on the back end too, preventing law enforcement from seeing a dealer's activity even after identification.
The suit also criticizes Snapchat's screenshot notifications, geolocation of users and algorithms suggesting connections based on demographics.
Snap filed a motion to dismiss citing Section 230 of the Communications Decency Act; a hearing was scheduled for 18 October.
A Snap spokesperson said the company works to 'block search results for drug-related terms' and redirects at-risk users to resources on fentanyl dangers.
Perla Mendoza's reports about her son Daniel (Elijah) Figueroa's dealer went unanswered, and it took eight months for Snap to flag the account.

Amy Neville's son Alexander died at 14 after taking a counterfeit Oxycontin tablet obtained through the app; he had told his parents he wanted help, and they planned rehab for the next day but did not take the pills away.
Ed Ternan, whose 21-year-old son Charlie died in April 2020 after taking a counterfeit Percocet bought on Snapchat, did not join the suit and calls it 'looking backwards'.
Ternan works full time with his wife on educating parents about fentanyl and has partnered with Snap on awareness campaigns, calling it 'a very successful partnership'.
Mendoza works to spread fentanyl awareness to Spanish-speaking families, and Neville visits schools and hosts monthly online meetings for peer-to-peer youth outreach.
